title: CLO 2025 Academic Month Practical Course to Cultivate High-Quality 3D Talent
description: CLO 2025 Official Academic Monthly Course Review Now Available! Professor Cate Latham from Virginia Commonwealth University, together with outstanding graduate Khistian Settle, provides a detailed explanation of the necessity of training 3D talent for the fashion industry.
transcript:
Okay, my name is Kate Latham. I'm an assistant professor from Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, Virginia. With me is Christian Settle, a former student of mine, recent graduate and independent contractor in 3D design.

A little bit about our department specifically: our current cohort is about this size right now. We have 200 merchandising students, 100 design students, and 97 merchandising minors. We also have two additional, including myself, so three total accredited academic CLO instructors. We are one of the first schools to begin implementing this new badge that CLO is issuing. Any student who graduates the CLO course with an average of 86 and above will receive this badge, which they can then share on LinkedIn and any platform where they want exposure.

I'd like to start off, before I explain the breakdown of the course that I teach, by talking a little bit about the course itself—why students need to know about 3D, why it's so important, and why they should prioritize it in their lives. Everyone already knows the sustainability aspect—that's a given, an obvious factor. It cuts down on time, waste, cost, everything. But in addition to that, you want to give them some practical information to get them excited.

We have seen, although the numbers are somewhat hard to come by, that from the most recent assessments by various sources, almost half of a survey of 60 luxury brands have claimed to begin incorporating technologies like AR and VR into their marketing and other parts of their production. Additionally, 30% of fashion brands have started implementing 3D processes in their production workflows.

Something very tangible for students to take in is that there are currently over 1,400 job listings related to 3D apparel design across four different job platforms. Considering the estimated 2,100 annual job openings in this field, that represents a large percentage of the opportunities available. This is encouraging and a strong reason to become proficient in 3D.

Thank you.

My teaching approach is as follows. It ultimately breaks down into what I call exercises in the classroom—a very structured, step-by-step process where we go through certain tools and functions in the software. It is very criteria-based: students submit screenshots of their work at different stages so I can check it off. Then we move into project-based learning: how to start applying these tools and functions in a project setting.

We also encourage the use of other software that can supplement CLO, such as Blender, obviously Adobe programs like Illustrator and Photoshop, which help a lot, and then really powerful programs like Unreal Engine.

More specifically, I like to focus on the interface and navigation first. The student needs to know how to get around the program foremost. Then we focus on tools, in the order that they are relevant in the workflow of a creative individual, specifically in fashion. We also focus on garment production: these tools feed into pattern making and actually building the garment. Each garment requires different tools, know-how, processes, and operations, so the skills compound with each garment we do.

Simultaneously, we develop our creative concept for project-based learning, where students begin researching target demographics, create a persona, and build an entire concept to guide their designs.

At the end of the course, we focus on advanced techniques like high-quality renders of still shots as well as animation. We bring in motion files and again discuss supplementary software, such as Daz for creating new or custom avatars, Blender, and others.

The content we planned to leave on a page was for the Violet class, where we started data analytics and a project looking across a range of different styles. We began with custom tools and operations intended to give students the best understanding of how to use CLO in real-world scenarios, whether in their own individual design processes or under an employer.

The workflow for our four-month semester is broken down at the bottom of the slide. In the first month, we go through exercises one through seven. We hold discussions during the first two months, roughly once a month. In these discussions, I like to talk about AI—ethics, of course—and how we should be using AI and emerging technologies as creatives. We also work on personas or character profiles depending on the final prompt for that semester.

By month two, we finish our exercises—usually about 10 to 12 for the semester—and then move into the more creative part, where students develop their entire collection. They conduct trend research, pull together design elements, finishings, and fabrications to build a collection.

The bullet point list at the top shows a specific sequence I like to follow with these exercises, focusing on the order most relevant to their workflow.

Some examples of exercises include working with elastic properties and waste pans, the 3D Pen Tool for bodycon patterns—a very helpful tool since not everyone has the right tools or full pattern-making knowledge. This tool makes patterns just by drawing on the avatar, which is very powerful.

We also do custom fabrics. One exercise asks students to create their own maps: diffuse/color maps, normal maps, displacement maps, and sometimes opacity maps.

The current final prompt for the semester is called "Designing for the Modern Professional." We aim to address the challenges modern professionals face: working long days, needing wearability and comfort, with sustainability ingrained in everything. Another twist is the challenge of convertibility—offering consumers multiple styles or a range of styles in a single garment.

Students can choose between two focuses in the final stage: a digital direction or a fully digital one. The main difference is that both involve designing and building, but the digital focus leads to a five-look capsule collection with physical garments, while the fully digital path focuses more on video campaigns, animation rendering, line sheets, lookbooks, and potentially a virtual showroom.

We also emphasize technology and tech packs because these are highly relevant in the industry. Tech packs are essential for any fashion work, and CLO can generate them automatically nowadays.

Moving on to an example of student work—Christian’s project when he took this class. For the final, students create a slide deck, essentially a pitch deck for their entire concept and collection. We were still using the final prompt inspired by video games, and Christian chose a particular video game for that semester. There’s a mood board for his project that’s a bit like a puzzle.

His character profile explains the character all design decisions center around, including the concept or ethos, color palette, fabrication, and the lineup of all five looks. Sometimes not all designs work perfectly. There are atomic, opal-like combinations visible, with misplacements and distortions, reminiscent of certain Persian styles.

Another component of the final project is printing full-scale patterns from CLO and creating physical garments. A key point I emphasize from the beginning is that CLO isn’t a magic tool for creating first-time-right garments. The 3D mesh is deceptive, and we have to train our eyes to recognize that we’re not creating a physical garment in the software. We must develop an eye for spotting fit issues.

On the left here is a PDF of some of Christian’s patterns and the pants made from them. I’ve also included garments from other students.

There are three main ways I like to use CLO that I want to share. First, if your department has specific blocks or slopers you use, it’s worthwhile to digitize them and work with those exact slopers in CLO to align digital and real-world work.

Second, CLO is amazing for exploring and experimenting with iconic, historic garments that otherwise you wouldn’t have time to study, touch, cut into, or apply new fabrics to. It’s a great way for students and young designers to learn from existing garments.

Third, I use CLO in my other courses for demonstrations. Tailoring, for example, is complex with many nuances in pattern drafting for jackets. Giving students a comprehensive idea of the goal helps them digest each step more easily. CLO can be a tool for conventional studio demos but also a powerful tool for students in their early twenties with little prior knowledge, enabling them to create many different things.

It’s a great way to engage students and ensure they understand CLO.

Lastly, some challenges and solutions. CLO is a massive program and can be intimidating. Sometimes students experience impostor syndrome, feeling they don’t belong. What helps, in my experience, is constantly reiterating core concepts, how the program works, and reminding them that main functions are always in the property editor or accessed via simple right-click menus.

Providing written and video tutorials has been very helpful. Students express how much they use resources provided by instructors specifically tailored to what they’re doing in class, even though many CLO tutorials exist online. Being able to review material anytime is helpful.

I also reassure students that about midway through the semester, the program “clicks.” Up until that point, many students feel frustrated or discouraged because the program is difficult and they may not grasp it as quickly as others. But there’s always a point where it becomes comfortable, like a learning plateau, and afterward, they feel capable of doing anything with the tools and functions.

There are many ways to achieve the same goal in CLO, just like other software such as Illustrator and Photoshop. It’s about solving problems in the way your brain understands. If you know how to do it in the real world, you can likely do it in CLO as well.

Technical limitations students face include the large processing power CLO requires. When using advanced functions such as animation, students often encounter computer issues or program crashes. Some have had their computers fail entirely mid-course.

If the department can provide additional computers or a computer lab, it’s very helpful.

I also advise students not to underestimate the time required for animation rendering in 3D. It takes an exceptional, sometimes abnormal, amount of time.

Lastly, understanding that the 3D mesh is highly deceptive when assessing garment fit is crucial. Just because a garment looks correct in simulation doesn’t mean printing the patterns will yield a well-fitting garment. Multiple steps are required to get as close as possible to a first-time-right sample.

Okay, I would like to introduce Christian Settle, and I’ll let you take it away, Christian.

---

All right, thank you. Hello, my name is Christian, and I’m a freelance 3D fashion designer specializing in sustainable digital design.

A little backstory: I never really expected to be in the fashion industry at all. I spent a lot of time doing graphic design and some 3D rendering with Blender and similar tools, making mock-ups of T-shirts and hoodies because I thought they were cool. Then I realized I wanted to elevate my understanding of fashion, which led me to VCU. Through my time there, I learned a lot of basics and fundamentals—it was amazing.

In my senior year, I enrolled in the CLO 3D class, and that truly changed how I thought about fashion design. I thought, “Wow, this is perfect. I know a little about 3D rendering, so let’s do this.” The software allowed me to visualize and have unlimited potential for experimenting. Being able to see and edit things in real time made a huge difference.

I’ve always been passionate about sustainability. The department emphasized it heavily. I took a sustainability class where we learned about overproduction and overconsumption. I wanted to make a difference but felt lost on how to incorporate sustainability into my design process. CLO 3D helped me slow down without impacting deadlines.

I was able to create virtual environments and print patterns, saving significant time and money in sampling—a crucial factor for me as a student.

Those two benefits greatly boosted my productivity. Even talking with peers, they often say it’s expensive to buy software weekly, but CLO saved me a lot of money in that respect. I’m very grateful for what CLO 3D has given me.

Post-graduation, I started a career with CLO 3D. I do technical design; everything I do is within CLO 3D. I help brands with visual prototyping and fashion solutions, whether that’s patterns, tech packs, or merchandising renders. CLO helps me demonstrate to brands how cost-effective it is and how much time and money it saves.

Here are some ways I help brands: I do 3D design and sampling, quickly creating digital garments to reduce or eliminate the need for physical samples. I streamline the design process, speeding things up by showing garments in real time and quickly changing seam lines, style lines, or entire garments with fast turnaround.

I also do pattern making and technical design. I take their patterns, put them into CLO, and pinpoint where garments need alterations or additions, like facings.

Additionally, I generate tech packs, spec out garments, export files, and send them to brands for manufacturing.

Of course, I also do 3D renders and animations. I started with creating high-quality renders using CLO, but I also use Blender and Unreal Engine for more realistic lighting or full video campaigns. This is valuable for marketing materials, websites, and social media.

That’s it.

chunks.content: --- ## CLO 3D Exercises and Final Project Focus This section provides examples of exercises used in the course and describes the semester’s final project themes and expectations. Exercises include working with elastic properties, waste pans, and the 3D Pen Tool for bodycon patterns, which allows pattern creation directly on avatars without extensive pattern-making knowledge. Students also create custom fabric maps: diffuse/color maps, normal maps, displacement maps, and opacity maps. The semester’s final prompt, “Designing for the Modern Professional,” addresses challenges like long workdays, wearability, comfort, sustainability, and garment convertibility—offering multiple styles in one garment. Students choose between two final project paths: - **Digital Direction:** Design and build a five-look capsule collection with physical garments. - **Fully Digital:** Focus on video campaigns, animation rendering, line sheets, lookbooks, and virtual showrooms. The course emphasizes the creation and use of tech packs, which CLO can now generate automatically, reflecting their critical role in industry workflows. --- ## Student Project Example and Practical Use of CLO 3D This section showcases student work and practical strategies for integrating CLO 3D into fashion education and design processes. Christian Settle’s final project involved creating a pitch deck centered on a video game-inspired concept. His mood board, character profile, color palette, fabrication choices, and five-look lineup guided design decisions. The project displayed experimental patterns with unique combinations and occasional intentional misplacements, reminiscent of Persian styles. Students print full-scale patterns from CLO and construct physical garments, recognizing CLO 3D is not a “magic tool” for flawless first-time samples. The 3D mesh simulation can be deceptive, necessitating a trained eye to identify fit issues. Three recommended uses of CLO 3D include: 1. **Digitizing Departmental Blocks/Slopers:** Aligning digital and physical garment development. 2. **Exploring Historic Garments:** Experimenting with iconic styles without damaging originals. 3. **Demonstrations in Other Courses:** Enhancing understanding of tailoring and complex pattern drafting through visual tools. These approaches engage students with varying levels of experience and help them grasp complex concepts effectively. --- ## Challenges, Solutions, and Technical Considerations This section discusses common challenges students face learning CLO 3D and strategies to overcome them, along with technical limitations of the software. CLO 3D’s complexity can cause impostor syndrome among students. Repeatedly reinforcing core concepts, simplifying navigation (property editor and right-click menus), and providing tailored written and video tutorials help ease learning. Students typically experience a learning plateau mid-semester, after which proficiency increases dramatically. Multiple paths exist to achieve the same result in CLO, similar to Adobe software, allowing users to solve problems in ways that suit their thinking. Technical challenges include high processing power requirements, especially for animation rendering, which can cause crashes and hardware failures. Providing departmental computer labs or additional machines mitigates this issue. Students are cautioned not to underestimate the time needed for animation rendering. Finally, the deceptive nature of the 3D mesh requires multiple iterations to approach a well-fitting physical garment, emphasizing the importance of skillful pattern evaluation.

Finally, the deceptive nature of the 3D mesh requires multiple iterations to approach a well-fitting physical garment, emphasizing the importance of skillful pattern evaluation. --- ## Christian Settle: Career Experience Using CLO 3D This section provides insight from Christian Settle, a freelance 3D fashion designer, on how CLO 3D shaped his skills and career in sustainable digital fashion design. Christian’s background includes graphic design and 3D rendering with Blender. Enrolling in the CLO 3D course at VCU transformed his approach to fashion design by enabling real-time visualization and expansive experimentation. Sustainability was a core departmental focus. CLO 3D helped Christian slow down the design process without affecting deadlines, saving time and money on physical sampling. Post-graduation, Christian works entirely within CLO 3D, offering services such as: - 3D design and virtual sampling to reduce physical sample needs. - Streamlining design processes with rapid garment modifications. - Pattern making and technical design assessment to refine garment fit. - Generating tech packs and exporting manufacturing files. - Producing high-quality renders and animations, supplemented by Blender and Unreal Engine for enhanced visuals used in marketing and campaigns. Christian credits CLO 3D for significant productivity gains and cost savings in his freelance work, emphasizing its value in sustainable fashion workflows.
